summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Atlas Financial through Optimize recommendations: batching configuration, prefix vs KV cache tradeoffs, and a cost model showing unit token savings at various batch sizes. Customer is interested in a pilot; key concerns are latency SLOs for synchronous API calls and audit logs/KMS for PII-sensitive prompts.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, good to see you all. we'll run through batching and kv cache optimizations and a simple cost model.
[00:12] Priya Shah: thanks lena, excited. quick context — we run customer support summarization and risk scoring, latencies target is sub-300ms 95, volume spikes morning/afternoon.
[00:28] Marco Diaz: cool, that helps. quick question on payloads — are prompts long? do you include whole chat history or just recent turns?
[00:36] Tom Reynolds: mostly recent 2 turns, sometimes we attach last 5 messages for complex cases, average tokens ~450 per request.
[00:44] Marco Diaz: got it. that changes batching behavior. so starting with batching basics — we recommend dynamic batching up to a latency SLO threshold. e.g., if you can tolerate 150ms extra queuing we can batch to N=8 and see big token cost wins.
[01:05] Avery Li: sorry, can you define dynamic batching?
[01:08] Lena Park: yeah, dynamic batching means the runtime aggregates individual requests into a single GPU batch until either batch size or a max wait timer is hit. it's workload-aware so busy periods hit target batches, quiet periods low latency.
[01:22] Priya Shah: and kv cache/prefix cache? is that different from batching?
[01:26] Marco Diaz: yes, different layer. prefix cache (we also call kv cache sometimes) stores key/value states for repeated prefixes so subsequent tokens don't re-compute earlier transformer states. good for repeated prompts — e.g., a template of instruction + user info.
[01:45] Tom Reynolds: we do a lot of templated prompts for compliance checks, so that sounds promising.
[01:49] Marco Diaz: exactly. the tradeoff is memory vs compute. KV cache reduces per-token compute but increases memory usage per session.
[02:02] Lena Park: we showed a simple cost model earlier in the deck — putting numbers: with batch size 1 you pay X, with batch size 8 you can reduce per-token GPU-seconds by ~35-45% depending on model and sequence length. adding kv cache on top reduces generation cost another 10-25% if prompt prefixes repeat often.
[02:24] Priya Shah: are those numbers measured on your hosted infra or dedicated?
[02:27] Marco Diaz: measured on a mix — our public benchmarks are on hosted GPU clusters but we profile across instance types. with Dedicated the savings pattern is similar but tail latency guarantees improve.
[02:39] Priya Shah: latency is our primary concern; we can accept some batching if P95 stays under 300ms.
[02:47] Marco Diaz: understood. we can target a max batching wait timer of 20ms which usually yields batches of 2-4 in your traffic pattern and keeps P95 in the 200-280ms range for 7B-class models.
[03:01] Tom Reynolds: curious about warm/cold sessions for KV cache. how long does Redwood keep KV cache entries?
[03:07] Marco Diaz: retention is configurable; we typically keep per-session KV for up to 5-30 minutes, and you can set eviction policies. for Atlas's use case I'd suggest a 10-minute TTL and an LRU eviction to balance memory.
[03:20] Avery Li: what about multi-tenant memory isolation? we need guarantees for data separation.
[03:25] Lena Park: good point. on Dedicated or Private deployments, KV memory is isolated per-customer instance. on hosted we use tenant-aware namespaces and encryption at rest; audit logs show evictions. we'll share the security docs.
[03:39] Priya Shah: perfect. can you walk through the cost model again with a concrete example?
[03:43] Marco Diaz: sure. assume 1M requests/month, average input 450 tokens, output 60 tokens. with no batching, compute tokens ~510M tokens generated and model latencies give you baseline cost of $Y. with batching N=4 we reduce GPU utilization per token and that maps to approx 28% cost reduction. add KV cache that avoids recomputing 200 tokens on average for repeated prefixes — another 12% savings, so combined ~36% cheaper than baseline. (note: approximate and varies by model/hardware).
[04:25] Tom Reynolds: those are attractive numbers. how do we measure quality regressions if we change quantization or batching?
[04:30] Marco Diaz: we run evals with your owned prompt set. Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitors and regression alerts: you pin a baseline evaluation set and we track metrics after deployments. we'll tie alerts to rollbacks.
[04:45] Priya Shah: i need clarity on when batching could affect output ordering or token streaming. we show streaming to client, is that impacted?
[04:52] Marco Diaz: streaming works but if you batch, earliest tokens in a batch are streamed first once computed; however there can be additional micro-latency due to batching window. if streaming latency is critical, we can route those requests to low-latency pool (Dedicated small instances) or set batching timers to near-zero.
[05:12] Avery Li: any configuration UI in Console for these options?
[05:15] Lena Park: yes — Console -> Optimize -> Batching shows suggested batch sizes, simulation graphs, and a slider to set max wait timer and target latency. KV cache settings are in the same view, including TTL and eviction.
[05:29] Priya Shah: you mentioned autoscaling interactions — will batching cause spiky GPU usage?
[05:33] Marco Diaz: batching smooths instantaneous GPU usage but can increase sustained throughput; autoscaling policies should be configured to scale on token throughput rather than request count. we recommend scale-up thresholds on GPU utilization and scale-down on sustained low token rates.
[05:50] Tom Reynolds: about metrics — what per-token telemetry do we get?
[05:53] Lena Park: you get token-level cost, per-route latency distributions, batching efficiency (effective tokens per batch), cache hit rates, and per-model throughput.
[06:05] Marco Diaz: quick demo — (screen share noise) so here's the Optimize tab. slide: a simulated traffic trace, recommended batches highlighted, expected cost savings. you can upload your sample traces and run a cost sim.
[06:28] Marco Diaz: notice the left pane shows suggested batching histogram; right pane is KV cache hit rate estimate based on your sample prompts. we've run a quick estimate on the sample you provided earlier — 18% KV hit predicted.
[06:43] Priya Shah: the sample we uploaded was small; what's the margin of error?
[06:47] Marco Diaz: depends — for templated prompts 10-20% error; for varied user-generated prompts more variance. best to run 1-2 week pilot with real traffic.
[06:58] Avery Li: can Optimize suggest a per-route policy? e.g., route /api/summarize to higher batch but /api/live to low-latency?
[07:05] Marco Diaz: yes, per-route policy is supported. Console allows you to set routing policies by endpoint, and we can set fallbacks to a low-latency pool.
[07:13] Tom Reynolds: about eviction — if eviction causes cache churn, is there a way to pre-warm the cache?
[07:18] Marco Diaz: you can pre-warm by replaying recent sessions during low-traffic windows or call a cache-warm API. also you can pin some prefixes.
[07:26] Priya Shah: security question — are KV cache entries encrypted in-memory?
[07:30] Lena Park: in-memory encryption depends on deployment. on Private you can integrate with HSM/KMS for encryption keys; on hosted we encrypt at rest and use tenant namespaces, plus audit logs. we'll send the SOC2 docs and KMS integration notes.
[07:44] Marco Diaz: ok here's a proposed pilot: Dedicated small pool, enable dynamic batching with max wait 20ms, batch cap 8, KV TTL 10min, run pilot for 2 weeks, evaluate costs and P95.
[07:58] Priya Shah: that sounds reasonable. can you also include a runbook for rollback if there are regressions?
[08:03] Lena Park: yes — we'll include rollback playbook and mention automatic fallback to a less-optimized model variant.
[08:11] Tom Reynolds: who owns the pilot engineering tasks?
[08:13] Priya Shah: our infra team (tom) for network/VPC; ML team (me) for prompt sets; product (avery) to validate UX.
[08:22] Marco Diaz: I'll handle the Redwood side: initial config, run the benchmark, and share results. Lena will handle commercial and security docs.
[08:30] Avery Li: what success metrics should we track?
[08:33] Marco Diaz: cost per 1k requests, P95 latency, cache hit rate, quality regressions (ROUGE/accuracy) on evaluation set.
[08:40] Priya Shah: timeline — we want pilot next week if possible.
[08:43] Lena Park: we'll aim to kick off on Monday. I'll send calendar invite after call and attach the cost model spreadsheet.
[08:51] Marco Diaz: small note — for your 450-token inputs, quantization choices (4-bit) can also reduce memory and increase batching efficiency but we should run quality evals before enabling.
[09:03] Tom Reynolds: what's the overhead of enabling KV cache on memory footprint?
[09:07] Marco Diaz: roughly each cached prefix stores KV pairs proportional to model layers and sequence length; for 450 tokens you might see ~200-400MB per active session for 13B-class models — 7B-class is less. that's why TTL and eviction matter.
[09:25] Avery Li: we'd likely go 7B for cost reasons, can you replicate numbers on that class?
[09:30] Marco Diaz: yes, we'll benchmark on 7B and provide per-instance memory and expected hit-rate savings.
[09:36] Priya Shah: any legal/contract blockers we should be aware of?
[09:39] Lena Park: standard NDA exists; for Private deployments there are platform fees and support tiers — we'll include pricing in the sheet.
[09:47] Priya Shah: great. last ask — can you include the sample cost sim as a csv?
[09:51] Lena Park: yes, cost model csv and a slide deck.
[09:54] Marco Diaz: closing recap: Redwood to send pricing and security docs (Lena), Redwood to run benchmark and propose batching/KV settings (Marco), Atlas to provide sample requests and approve pilot kickoff date (Priya/Avery/Tom).
[10:10] Priya Shah: thanks everyone, appreciate the pragmatic approach.
[10:14] Lena Park: thanks all, talk soon.
[10:16] (call ends)
